# Ovid — Metamorphoses I–VIII (Miller, second edition 1921; consulted 1951 impression)

[Source index](../../../README.md) · [Reading entrance](../../../../../../README.md) · [48 movements](../../../../../../section-rooms/README.md)

## Chicago 18 forms

**Full note:** Ovid, *Metamorphoses*, vol. 1, *Books I–VIII*, trans. Frank Justus Miller, 2 nd ed. (1921; repr., Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press; London: William Heinemann, 1951), 1.452–567, [digital text](https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Metamorphoses_(Miller)/Book_I).

**Shortened note:** Ovid, *Metamorphoses*, 1.452–567.

**Bibliography:** Ovid. *Metamorphoses*. Vol.1, *Books I–VIII*. Translated by Frank Justus Miller.2 nd ed.1921. Reprint, Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press; London: William Heinemann, 1951. https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Metamorphoses_(Miller)/Book_I.

## Essay use and intact relation

This house supports `mytheme-apollo-eros-daphne-peneus`, whose admitted destination is `submission-package/essay/symbolon/mytheme/worlds/roman-latin/apollo-eros-daphne-peneus/WHOLE.md`. Native 020's form/possession/Other operation bears A19's local arbitration, A20's image/valuation and A27's unity without possession. Historical citation establishes the narrated relation; it does not prove the essay's philosophical interpretation or equate Apollo with a universal theory of cognition.

The whole requires Python and Apollo's boast, Cupid's contrary arrows, Daphne's unmarried orientation and paternal request, the chase, transformation, recoil and the laurel's public office. Her earlier-narrated request need not be asserted as chronologically before Cupid's arrow. The ending's seeming assent must remain beside the recoil. Their tension gives the native reading something determinate to interpret rather than permission to omit an inconvenient line.

## Material metadata and access provenance

- **Selected edition:** Miller's second edition 1921; consulted 1951 impression as digitally transcribed, not Goold's later revision.
- **Edition determination:** [title leaf, scan-page 7](https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Page:Metamorphoses.djvu/7) explicitly reads MCMLI with Harvard/Heinemann; [printing leaf, scan-page 8](https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Page:Metamorphoses.djvu/8) states first 1916, second 1921 and subsequent printings through 1951. Read 2026-09-06. These primary leaf transcriptions take precedence over the file catalogue's general 1921 date. Image requests returned 403; no image collation claimed.
- **Full passage read:** Miller Book I digital paragraphs covering 1.416–567, including every Apollo/Daphne paragraph and the closing sentence, 2026-09-06. [Stable consulted transcription revision](https://en.wikisource.org/w/index.php?title=Metamorphoses_(Miller)/Book_I&oldid=13715118).
- **Separate Latin locator witness:** [BCS, 1.416–567](https://bcs.fltr.ucl.ac.be/metam/Met01/M01-416-567.html), Boxus/Poucet 2005 French translation with Latin. It confirms line segmentation, not Miller English wording. BCS marks a textual gap at 546; do not silently fill it from another edition.
- **Local copy:** no complete book mirrored; primary full-text links remain available. NOTES absent; none created.

## Passage card — `ovid-1921-metamorphoses-miller-q001` — boast, arrows and refusal
^ovid-1921-metamorphoses-miller-q001

Apollo's victory precedes his taunt; Cupid answers through opposed arrows. Daphne asks Peneus for unmarried life after Diana's example.

- **Locator:**1.438–489; whole generative prelude 1.416–451.
- **Status:** paraphrase-ready from consulted digital edition; no quotation supplied.
- **Verification:** Miller full passage read 2026-09-06; line route checked against BCS.
- **Source relation:** paraphrased.
- **Evidential action:** supports the whole relation before the chase.
- **Consumers:** `mytheme-apollo-eros-daphne-peneus`; A20; A27.
- **Use boundary:** retain Cupid and Peneus as agents; the source does not prove that every act of delineation is possessive.

<a id="ovid-1921-metamorphoses-miller-q002"></a>
## Passage card — `ovid-1921-metamorphoses-miller-q002` — powers fail to obtain the Other
^ovid-1921-metamorphoses-miller-q002

Apollo invokes prophecy, music, archery and medicine. Daphne flees; exhausted, she appeals for transformation.

- **Locator:**1.490–552.
- **Status:** paraphrase-ready from consulted digital edition.
- **Verification:** read in Miller 2026-09-06 with BCS line sequence; the BCS546 gap is retained as a witness distinction.
- **Source relation:** paraphrased; native form/possession argument is argued from this scene.
- **Evidential action:** supports and qualifies.
- **Consumers:** `mytheme-apollo-eros-daphne-peneus`; A19; A20; A27.
- **Use boundary:** do not narrate pursuit as a mutually desired romance or make Peneus a doctrine of QL's zero.

<a id="ovid-1921-metamorphoses-miller-q003"></a>
## Passage card — `ovid-1921-metamorphoses-miller-q003` — recoil and the difficult ending
^ovid-1921-metamorphoses-miller-q003

> But even the wood shrank from his kisses.

- **Locator:**1.556; scene 1.553–567.
- **Status:** quotation-ready against the named digital transcription; print-image collation Open.
- **Verification:** exact nine-word sentence transcribed and reread 2026-09-06 from Miller Book I stable revision 13715118; Latin line 556 crosschecked in BCS. No uncertain OCR token in this sentence.
- **Source relation:** extracted.
- **Evidential action:** supports continued resistance; qualifies completion by possession.
- **Consumers:** `mytheme-apollo-eros-daphne-peneus`; A20; A27.
- **Use boundary:** Apollo assigns laurel an emblematic office; 566–567 then reports a seeming head-like assent. Do not delete that ambiguity or claim the poem explicitly resolves it as the essay does.
